D 32, 31 (1994), abstract (p. 31) and p. 32 (first two pages read in the publisher's preview): '7p 5P1' excited from 6s 3S1 at 591 nm and detected at 518 nm. Note: level identification derived here from the printed wavelengths: 46652.738 -> 63556.707 is 591.41 nm in air (591.58 nm vacuum) and 63556.707 -> 44253.000 is 517.89 nm in air (518.04 nm vacuum); the other NIST 5P1 level (b 5P1, 63669.944) would need 587.48 / 514.87 nm (air)

Zerne, Berzinsh, Svanberg, Z. Phys. D 32, 31 (1994), abstract (p. 31) and p. 32: level called '7p 5P2' by the authors, excited from 6s 3S1 at 588 nm and detected at 515 nm. Note: level identification derived here from the printed wavelengths, not from the authors' J label: 46652.738 -> 63669.944 is 587.48 nm in air (587.64 nm vacuum) and 63669.944 -> 44253.000 is 514.87 nm in air (515.01 nm vacuum), matching 588 / 515 nm; the NIST 5P2 level 63610.819 would need 589.53 / 516.44 nm (air), which would be printed as 590 / 516 nm. The other three levels of the paper reproduce the printed wavelengths to within 0.5 nm with NIST energies (579 / 508, 573 / 504, 591 / 518 nm), which supports the identification. NIST (Morillon and Verges classification) labels 63669.944 'b 5P1' (J = 1) while Zerne et al. call the level 5P2: J assignment in conflict, see 'conflicts'
